# Diagnosing No Heat in Car Blowers: Beyond the Thermostat

A Nissan Qashqai 1.5 dci that isn't overheating but delivers cold air from the vents presents a classic thermal management puzzle. The immediate instinct is often to blame the thermostat, assuming it has seized in the closed position. While a stuck thermostat is a valid suspect, your diagnosis of changing it and draining the system twice already rules out a simple blockage at the core of the engine loop. If the lower radiator hose and the bottom of the radiator remain cold while the upper hose feels warm or hot, you have successfully confirmed that coolant is circulating through the pump and reaching the radiator. The heat exchange failure is happening downstream of the radiator cap.

The root cause lies in how the cooling system is routed. In many modern engines, including the 1.5 dci found in your Qashqai, there is a specific valve called the heater control valve (or a blend door actuator in newer designs) that directs hot coolant into the heater core. If this valve remains closed or if the blend door is stuck, no matter how warm the coolant is inside the engine block, it will never reach the cabin. The fact that your radiator bottom is cold suggests the water pump is working and there are no major airlocks preventing circulation, but the path to the heater core might be physically obstructed or electronically gated.

Start by verifying the physical state of the heater control valve. Locate the hose running from the engine block to the firewall; this line should feel hot when the engine is at operating temperature and the fan is set to maximum. If you can locate this specific hose, touch it carefully (use a glove) while the car is idling with the AC off. If it is cold, the valve is likely stuck closed or has failed mechanically. Replacing this component is often cheaper than a head gasket repair, but it requires checking for external leaks around the valve body as well.

If your vehicle uses an electronic blend door actuator rather than a manual valve, the issue shifts to the HVAC control module. The symptoms of a failed actuator include cold air blowing even when the dial is set to hot, or air that cycles unpredictably between hot and cold. In these cases, you can often diagnose the fault by listening for the clicking sound of an actuator struggling to move the flap, or by scanning the instrument cluster for HVAC-related error codes.

Another common pitfall involves air pockets trapped in the heater core itself. Even if you drained the system twice, air can get trapped in the highest point of the loop, which is often the heater core located deep inside the dashboard. To purge this without removing the unit, locate the heater core bleed valve (often a small plastic nut near the firewall). Open it while the engine is running and the cooling system is hot; if air hisses out before fluid flows steadily, you have found your culprit.

Do not overlook the possibility of a clogged heater core despite the lack of overheating. If debris or rust flakes accumulate in the narrow tubes of the heater core, flow restriction occurs. This can be tested by swapping the inlet and outlet hoses at the firewall (if the car has a manual valve) to see if performance improves. If the engine temperature is high but the cabin remains freezing, the core is likely blocked internally.

Finally, consider the cabin air filter. A severely clogged filter can restrict airflow through the heater core so much that even hot fluid cannot transfer sufficient warmth to raise the air temperature above ambient levels. Check and replace the filter if it appears saturated with dust or leaves. This is a low-cost intervention that often resolves "no heat" complaints without needing to dismantle the dashboard.

If you have verified the thermostat, water pump, heater core flow, and blend door actuation, and the issue persists, professional scanning for HVAC module communication errors may be required to pinpoint whether an electrical fault is preventing the system from engaging the heat cycle.
